gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the makers measure cycle life and peak power differently. BLUETTI's Apex 300 kit page quotes 6,000 cycles to 80% capacity retention and calls its 7,680 W figure "Lifting Power", with no surge rating. Anker's F3000 page gives 4,000 cycles with no end-of-life capacity at all and a separate 7,200 W "AC Surge Power". So neither the cycle counts nor the peak-watt numbers in the rival tables compare like for like.
standout_why: I opened StormWatts (cited) and EcoSolarKits (rank 4). StormWatts has no cycle-life or surge figures at all, but it already normalises solar input per port (HomePower 3000 500 W per port, 1,000 W dual; DELTA 3 Ultra 11–60 V, 18 A, 800 W), so the solar part of this angle is taken. EcoSolarKits lists bare cycle counts (HomePower 3000 4,000; Apex 300 6,000+) without the end-of-life percentage behind them. It also puts the Apex 300's 7,680 W in the same AC/surge column as Jackery's 7,200 W surge, though BLUETTI labels that figure "Lifting Power". EcoSolarKits already says the Apex 300 needs the SolarX 4K add-on for its large solar figure. UnpluggedWatts (cited), LightsOnLabs and SolarGenAdvisor failed with a TLS certificate error, so I could not check them. I could only source the end-of-life percentage for one kit, the Apex 300, so the footnote is incomplete.
decides: It does not change the pick. It adds a footnote to the table: the Apex 300's 6,000 cycles is the only count with a published end-of-life point (80%), and the Anker F3000 and BLUETTI Elite 300 counts have none, so a 6,000-vs-4,000 comparison cannot be ranked as if they meant the same thing. The Apex 300 kit is also a pre-order (store says late January), so the ships-now pick has to come from another kit regardless. The peak-power footnote matters for motor loads: BLUETTI's "Lifting Power" figures (7,680 W Apex 300, 4,800 W Elite 300) should not sit in a surge column next to Anker's 7,200 W "AC Surge Power".
